items.title: AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes report
items.why: Source of the quotation (p.24, recommendations for recruiters) and the figure (p.12). Also tells recruiters to seek assurance on training data (p.19), carry out due diligence and regular checks through the contract (p.40) and record controller and processor roles (pp.44-45). Covers data protection only.
items.quote: Request test results or reports and evidence of actions AI providers have taken to address fairness, accuracy, or bias issues in AI tools or outputs.

items.title: Thinking of using AI to assist recruitment? Our key data protection considerations
items.why: Six questions for buyers. Question 3: record roles in the contract and consider performance measures such as accuracy and bias targets. Question 4: seek clear assurances that bias has been mitigated and ask to see the documentation.
items.quote: You should seek clear assurances from the AI provider that they have mitigated bias and ask to see any relevant documentation.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 28: Processor
items.why: Controller may use only processors giving sufficient guarantees; the contract must let the controller audit and inspect. Applies only where the supplier is a processor, and only to data protection compliance. Read with Article 5(2), accountability.
items.quote: allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections, conducted by the controller or another auditor mandated by the controller

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 109: Liability of employers and principals
items.why: The duty is on the employer (s.39) and the service-provider (s.29); an agent's authorised acts are the principal's regardless of knowledge. Nothing in these sections mentions suppliers of software, so the application to bought AI is a reading, not a ruling.
items.quote: Anything done by an agent for a principal, with the authority of the principal, must be treated as also done by the principal.

items.title: Responsible AI in Recruitment
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Sections 3.2 (during procurement), 4.1 (before deployment), 4.2 (ongoing monitoring; iterative bias audits)
items.why: Questions to put to suppliers on training data and performance across groups; says a supplier should be able to evidence its claims; recommends a pilot because supplier data and the buyer's data differ. Contains nothing on contract terms.
items.quote: A supplier should be able to provide evidence of these claims to your team, regardless of your level of technical literacy.

items.title: Guidelines for AI procurement
items.locator: Sections 'Selection, evaluation and award' and 'Contract implementation and ongoing management'
items.why: Written for public buyers: avoid black-box systems, require process logs for auditability, test the model on an ongoing basis, plan for end of life in the contract. Dated June 2020 and not specific to fairness.
items.quote: You can also consider the requirement for independent audits of the algorithms.

items.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
items.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), published by Courts and Tribunals Judiciary
items.quote: SWP have never sought to satisfy themselves, either directly or by way of independent verification, that the software program in this case does not have
items.why: The one UK appellate ruling found on taking a supplier's fairness on trust. The police force relied on the manufacturer's evidence about its facial recognition software and could not see the training data, which the supplier treated as commercially confidential; the court held the force had not done all it reasonably could to check for race or sex bias. Decided under the public sector equality duty, so it binds public bodies and those carrying out public functions; it is not a ruling on a private employer's liability.

items.title: Review into bias in algorithmic decision-making
items.publisher: Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation
items.locator: Executive summary and Part III, passage on public sector procurement and the supply chain (before Recommendation 16); chapter 3, Recruitment
items.quote: there is limited maturity or consistency in contractual mechanisms to place responsibilities in the right place in the supply chain
items.why: The government's independent review of algorithmic bias. States that accountability for fair decisions stays with the body making them, and that contracts were not yet doing the work of passing duties to suppliers. The recruitment chapter describes how vendors test their own tools. Dated 2020; the finding on contracts is about the public sector.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, artificial intelligence toolkit: Contracts and third parties
items.locator: Second control measure (due diligence before procuring), list 'Ways to meet our expectations'
items.quote: do not procure the services or datasets if bias or discrimination cannot be mitigated
items.why: What the regulator's auditors expect of a buyer: decide the acceptable level of accuracy before buying, seek guarantees on the source of data and models, write accuracy measures into the contract, carry out an independent evaluation of trade-offs, and walk away if bias cannot be reduced. Voluntary audit toolkit, not law; under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act. No date on the page; year follows the existing library entry.

items.title: SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Prudential Regulation Authority, Bank of England
items.locator: Principle 2.6, 'Use of externally developed models, third-party vendor products', points (a)-(b), PDF p.19
items.quote: satisfy themselves that the vendor models have been validated to the same standards as their own internal MRM expectations
items.why: The clearest UK regulatory statement that a bought model must be checked like one built in-house: the board stays responsible, and the firm should verify the vendor's data and assumptions and monitor the model against its own outcomes. Supervisory expectation for banks, building societies and designated investment firms with internal model approval, in effect from 17 May 2024 (para 1.5); it is about model risk in general, not fairness in particular.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 13: Transparency and provision of information to deployers
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: when appropriate, its performance regarding specific persons or groups of persons on which the system is intended to be used
items.why: Where it applies, this turns the buyer's request for fairness evidence into the supplier's legal duty: the instructions for use of a high-risk system must give its performance for the groups it will be used on and describe the training, validation and testing data. 'When appropriate' leaves room for the supplier. The first pass could not read this article. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text (EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026), not the Official Journal. EU law: reaches UK firms only where a system or its output is used in the EU. No application date is stated here.

items.title: Automated Employment Decision Tools (Local Law 144 of 2021)
items.publisher: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
items.quote: prohibits employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool unless the tool has been subject to a bias audit within one year
items.why: International comparator. The first law to make independent verification of a hiring tool a condition of using it: a bias audit within the past year, with the results made public and notice to candidates. The duty falls on the employer, not the vendor. The enforcing department's summary page, not the text of the law; enforcement began 5 July 2023. New York City only.

items.title: Auditing Work: Exploring the New York City algorithmic bias audit regime
items.quote: we find that LL 144 has not effectively established an auditing regime
items.why: What happened when verification was mandated: interviews with 16 auditors and practitioners found loose definitions of the tools covered and of an independent auditor, and auditors struggling to get data from vendors. A warning that a bought audit report is not the same as assurance, and a reason to write data access into the contract. Small qualitative sample, one city, early in the regime; preprint as read.

items.title: Mitigating Bias in Algorithmic Hiring: Evaluating Claims and Practices
items.publisher: Manish Raghavan, Solon Barocas, Jon Kleinberg and Karen Levy (authors' copy on arXiv 1906.09208; published version DOI 10.1145/3351095.3372828)
items.quote: we document and analyze the claims and practices of companies offering algorithms for employment assessment
items.why: The standard study of what vendors of hiring algorithms say about bias and what they disclose about how their tools are built and validated. Shows what a buyer can and cannot learn from a supplier's public statements. Based on vendors' published material, not on testing the tools; United States law and market.

items.title: What does it mean to 'solve' the problem of discrimination in hiring? Social, technical and legal perspectives from the UK on automated hiring systems
items.publisher: Javier Sánchez-Monedero, Lina Dencik and Lilian Edwards (authors' copy on arXiv 1910.06144)
items.quote: such claims of bias mitigation are rarely scrutinised and evaluated
items.why: The UK counterpart: examines how three hiring systems in regular use in the UK describe, validate and audit their own bias controls, and sets those claims against UK equality and data protection law, which differ from the United States law the tools were designed around. Based on publicly available documents for three products, not on independent testing.
